newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya sees mild economic growth,says rates too high.
newsitem.headline: Kenya sees mild economic growth,says rates too high.

text.p: Kenya, forecasting mild economic growth in 1997, on Tuesday described its infrastructure as dilapidated and said real interest rates were too high for business.
Vice-President George Saitoti told a news conference that a drought from October to March had caused an increase in the budget deficit and a slow-down in gross domestic product (GDP) growth.
He saw GDP growth at 5.2 percent in 1997, down from 4.6 percent in 1996 and lower than earlier projections of 7.0 percent. The 1996 rate of 4.6 percent was lower than forecasts of 5.5 percent.

"The government is very much concerned about the very high interest rates for the simple reason that it is extremely difficult to borrow from commercial banks and other financial intermediaries for the purpose of development," Saitoti said.

"It is very difficult to get returns that will be able to meet the interest accrued that are quite high," Saitoti added. "This is an issue that is being approached cautiously. We will bring down the rates at a certain percentage."
Saitoti said there was a substantial amount of hard currency in the economy from foreign investors and a sharp reduction in interest rates would lead to "a very swift capital flight".
Lending rates for commercial banks are about 25-35 percent. Mortgage rates stand at 30-40 percent. Benchmark rates on 91-day government treasury bills have settled at 21 percent this year.
Saitoti, also minister for planning and national development, blamed a freeze on donor development funds for Kenya between 1991 and 1993 for a major infrastructure setback.
"Our own infrastructure is in a very terrible state of affairs. Terribly dilapidated," Saitoti told reporters.
Saitoti said cash from donors for the power, roads, water and other development sectors had just began to arrive and the rehabilitation of infrasture was just getting back on track.
"On top of current World Bank financing, there should be a separate topping up for our infrastructure initiative. We cannot achieve our set aims unless we develop this sector," he added.

Saitoti said negotiations with the United States on export quotas for textiles were continuing. He said a problem was that unscrupulous traders had abused the quota margins but Kenya was committed to punishing such corrupt traders fully.

Saitoti said single digit inflation of 1995 and 1996 would be maintained in 1997 on recovery of the agricultural sector following the start of seasonal long rains in April and pursuit of tight monetary policies by the Central Bank of Kenya.

Saitoti said expenditure in 1996/97 would rise to 148.08 billion shillings ($2.8 billion) versus 134.92 billion shillings in 1995/96. Spending compared with revenues projected at 148.82 billion shillings in 1996/97 from 143.64 billion shillings in 1995/96.
He said the overall government budget deficit was expected to be 7.12 billion shillings ($131.85 million) in 1996/97 in contrast to a surplus of 8.82 billion shillings in 1995/96.
He blamed government purchases of relief food because of drought and the need for national voter registration ahead of general elections later this year for the huge deficit.

Saitoti said better coffee and tea prices encouraged farmers while earnings from tourism and manufacturing were expected to rise. A recovery in demand in industrial countries meant that merchandise exports would increase through 1997, he added. ($ = 53.31 Kenyan Shillings)
